content: 1. The presence of flies around toilets, in food preparation areas, or near the eyes, as well as the presence of feces in or around a compound, were observed in sanitation studies. These studies showed mixed effects of sanitation interventions on most transmission pathways, with the majority showing no significant impact. 2. There was no evidence that sanitation interventions improved drinking water quality, reduced contamination of hands or sentinel toys, or decreased food, soil, or surface contamination. However, some evidence suggested that sanitation was associated with a reduction in fly populations and a decrease in visible feces, though these findings were not statistically significant. 3. Subgroup analyses indicated that sanitation interventions were more effective in reducing visible feces when initial sanitation coverage was low and when there was a significant difference in coverage between intervention and control groups. 4. Studies demonstrated an inverse relationship between the distance of a water source from a toilet and the level of fecal contamination in the water source. 5. Greater access to sanitation was associated with significantly lower odds of diarrhea, with a 12% reduction in all studies combined and a 23% reduction in intervention studies. Improved sanitation access also reduced the odds of infection with soil-transmitted helminths (STH) by 20–52%, depending on the specific parasite. 6. Sanitation access was protective against schistosomiasis and active trachoma and was positively associated with improved height-for-age outcomes. However, no significant effects were observed on weight-for-age or weight-for-height z-scores. 7. Freeman et al. (2017) reviewed the impact of sanitation interventions on infectious diseases (e.g., diarrhea, STH infections, schistosomiasis, trachoma) and nutritional outcomes. They included 171 eligible studies, 84 of which were part of meta-analyses. The quality of evidence was rated as low or very low due to substantial heterogeneity and reliance on observational designs. 8. Speich et al. (2016) reviewed the effects of sanitation and water treatment on intestinal protozoa infections, identifying 54 eligible studies. Sanitation availability or use was associated with significantly lower odds of infection with Entamoeba histolytica (44% reduction) and Giardia intestinalis (36% reduction), but no significant effects were observed for Blastocystis or Cryptosporidium. 9. Majorin et al. (2018) reviewed interventions to improve child feces disposal and their impact on diarrhea and STH infections. Safe disposal of child feces was associated with a 24% reduction in diarrhea odds when feces were disposed of in a toilet and a 46% reduction when children defecated in a toilet. However, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showed no significant impact on helminth infections. 10. Ejemot-Nwadiaro et al. (2015) reviewed handwashing promotion interventions and their effects on diarrhea. Handwashing promotion reduced diarrhea episodes by 30% in high-income countries and by 28% in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). However, long-term maintenance of handwashing habits remains poorly understood. 11. Yates et al. (2015) reviewed the impact of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions on people living with HIV, who are at higher risk of enteric infections. Lack of access to household sanitation was a significant risk factor, while toilet access was protective against intestinal parasites and diarrhea morbidity. 12. Sclar et al. (2017) reviewed the effects of sanitation on cognitive development and school absence. Improved household sanitation was generally associated with better cognitive outcomes, but the evidence on school absence was less clear and lacked a consistent pattern. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. 13. Sclar et al. (2018) examined the relationship between sanitation and well-being, focusing on aspects such as privacy, shame, anxiety, fear, assault, safety, dignity, and embarrassment. They identified 50 eligible studies, with a predominant focus on the experiences of women and girls. Results highlighted the importance of private sanitation facilities in improving well-being. 14. Overbo et al. (2016) reviewed the impacts of policy and programming strategies on sanitation adoption and sustained use. Political will, leadership, intersectoral coordination, and harmonized policies were critical for program success. Access to credit, when well-managed and coupled with community mobilization, also facilitated adoption. 15. Cultural norms and beliefs, such as the acceptance of open defecation, were significant barriers to sanitation adoption. Motivations for adoption varied by setting but often included privacy, shame, and social pressure. 16. Physical environmental factors, such as high water tables, seasonal flooding, and lack of space, were barriers to sanitation adoption. Implementation activities, including house visits, mass media campaigns, and education, were effective in raising awareness and demand for sanitation. 17. Monitoring and evaluation were essential for strategic planning and political accountability. Contextual factors influencing sanitation adoption and sustained use were interdependent, highlighting the need for effective planning and lesson-learning in program and policy implementation.
